# Comprehensive KPI Tracking & Reporting Framework"

*Prepared by: Zia U. Ahmed, Ph.D. • May 2026*


This document presents a comprehensive, end-to-end framework for
defining, tracking, and reporting Key Performance Indicators (KPIs) for
OALTC-licensed programs. The framework is structured around five
interconnected components: (1) strategic alignment and KPI governance,
(2) KPI taxonomy and definition standards, (3) data infrastructure and
pipeline architecture using Google BigQuery, (4) dashboard and reporting
design, and (5) continuous improvement and stakeholder engagement.
Together, these components equip the Bureau of Data Analytics and
Automation to deliver timely, accurate, and actionable performance
intelligence to OALTC program leaders, senior DOH leadership, and
external stakeholders.

The framework is designed to be scalable across all OALTC program types
— including nursing homes, assisted living programs, adult day services,
home care agencies, and continuing care retirement communities — and is
aligned with OALTC’s core strategic priorities of quality of care,
regulatory compliance, operational efficiency, workforce stability, and
health equity.

## Section 1: Strategic Alignment & KPI Governance

### 1.1 OALTC Strategic Priorities

All KPIs in this framework are anchored to OALTC’s five core strategic
priorities. Every metric must trace directly to at least one of these
pillars:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **\#** | **Strategic Pillar** | **Description** | **Primary Audience** |
| **1** | **Quality of Care** | Resident/client outcomes, safety events, care standard adherence across licensed facilities | Program Directors, DOH Leadership |
| **2** | **Regulatory Compliance** | Inspection outcomes, deficiency rates, complaint resolution timeliness, enforcement actions | Surveyors, Legal, Leadership |
| **3** | **Operational Efficiency** | Data submission compliance, processing times, workflow automation, cost-per-case metrics | Bureau Chiefs, IT, Finance |
| **4** | **Workforce Stability** | Staff turnover rates, vacancy rates, training completion across regulated providers | Program Managers, Workforce Unit |
| **5** | **Health Equity** | Disparity metrics by race, ethnicity, geography, payer type; access and outcome gaps across population groups | Health Equity Team, DOH Commissioner |

### 1.2 KPI Governance Structure

Robust KPI governance ensures accountability, consistency, and
continuous relevance of all metrics. The following three-tier governance
model is recommended:

- Tier 1 — Strategic KPIs: Reviewed by DOH senior leadership and OALTC
  Director on a quarterly basis. These are high-level outcome indicators
  tied directly to OALTC’s mission and reported in public-facing
  documents.

- Tier 2 — Operational KPIs: Reviewed by Bureau Chiefs and Program
  Managers monthly. These track day-to-day program performance and early
  warning signals.

- Tier 3 — Analytical KPIs: Reviewed by the Data Analytics team weekly.
  These are granular metrics used to monitor data quality, pipeline
  health, and emerging trends before they escalate.

- Each KPI is assigned a designated Data Owner (the program office
  responsible for the metric), a Data Steward (the analytics team member
  responsible for the data feed), and a Business Reviewer (the
  stakeholder who interprets and acts on the metric).

- A KPI Registry — maintained in a version-controlled document linked to
  the BigQuery metadata catalog — serves as the single source of truth
  for all active metrics, their definitions, data sources, owners, and
  update schedules.

## Section 2: KPI Taxonomy & Definition Standards

### 2.1 KPI Categories

KPIs are organized into four functional categories that span the full
program performance lifecycle:

- Outcome KPIs: Measure the end results of care and services (e.g.,
  hospitalization rates, resident satisfaction scores, deficiency
  citation counts).

- Process KPIs: Measure whether program activities are being executed as
  intended (e.g., timely completion of care assessments, inspection
  cycle adherence).

- Capacity KPIs: Measure resources and infrastructure (e.g., licensed
  bed occupancy, staff-to-resident ratios, data system uptime).

- Equity KPIs: Measure disparity and access gaps across demographic and
  geographic subgroups (e.g., outcome differentials by race/ethnicity or
  rural vs. urban location).

### 2.2 Master KPI Definition Template

Every KPI must be formally defined using the following standardized
template before it enters the tracking system. Consistency in definition
prevents misinterpretation and ensures comparability over time.

|  |  |
|----|----|
| **Field** | **Description / Example** |
| **KPI Name** | Hospital Readmission Rate within 30 Days |
| **Strategic Pillar** | Quality of Care |
| **KPI Category** | Outcome KPI |
| **Definition** | Percentage of nursing home residents discharged to a hospital who are readmitted within 30 days of initial discharge |
| **Numerator** | Count of residents readmitted to a hospital within 30 days of discharge from a nursing home |
| **Denominator** | Total count of nursing home discharges in the measurement period |
| **Formula** | (Numerator / Denominator) × 100 |
| **Unit of Measure** | Percentage (%) |
| **Data Source** | Medicaid claims data, MDS (Minimum Data Set), OALTC facility records in BigQuery |
| **Update Frequency** | Monthly |
| **Reporting Granularity** | Statewide, Regional, County, Facility-level |
| **Baseline Value** | Established from 3-year historical average (e.g., 18.2%) |
| **Target / Benchmark** | Reduce to ≤ 15% by FY2027; aligned with CMS national benchmark |
| **Warning Threshold** | Rate exceeds 20% for two consecutive months |
| **Data Owner** | Nursing Home Program Office |
| **Data Steward** | Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation |
| **Business Reviewer** | OALTC Director of Quality Improvement |
| **Limitations / Notes** | Exclude planned readmissions; flag facilities with \< 30 discharges as low-volume |

## Section 3: Data Infrastructure & Pipeline Architecture

### 3.1 Data Architecture Overview

The KPI tracking system is built on Google BigQuery as the central data
warehouse. The architecture follows a four-layer pipeline model:
Ingestion → Storage → Transformation → Presentation.

- Layer 1 — Ingestion: Raw data flows into BigQuery from OALTC-licensed
  program submissions, ITS-managed applications, Medicaid claims, MDS
  feeds, and survey system exports. Each data feed is assigned a schema,
  ingestion schedule, and validation ruleset.

- Layer 2 — Raw Storage (Data Lake): Unprocessed source data is stored
  in partitioned BigQuery tables by program, date, and source system.
  All raw records are retained for auditability and reprocessing.

- Layer 3 — Transformation (Data Mart): SQL-based ETL pipelines
  transform raw data into clean, analysis-ready tables. KPI
  calculations, denominator logic, and exclusion rules are encoded here
  using version-controlled SQL scripts or dbt models.

- Layer 4 — Presentation: Transformed KPI tables power dashboards
  (Looker Studio or Tableau), automated reports, and self-service query
  interfaces for OALTC program staff.

### 3.2 Data Quality Control Standards

Data quality is enforced at each pipeline stage using the following
six-dimension framework:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **Dimension** | **Definition** | **Validation Rule (Example)** | **Action if Failed** |
| **Completeness** | All required fields are populated | Null rate \< 2% for facility_id, report_date, and outcome fields | Flag record; alert Data Steward; exclude from KPI calc until resolved |
| **Validity** | Values fall within defined ranges and formats | Readmission rate between 0–100%; date format = YYYY-MM-DD | Reject record; log error; notify submitter |
| **Timeliness** | Data arrives within the expected submission window | Monthly feeds ingested by the 10th of the following month | Trigger escalation alert; mark period as provisional |
| **Consistency** | Values are consistent across linked tables and time periods | Facility bed count in submissions matches licensed capacity in registry | Flag discrepancy; hold for reconciliation |
| **Accuracy** | Values reflect real-world program activity | Outlier detection: z-score \> 3 triggers manual review | Queue for analyst review; annotate in dashboard |
| **Uniqueness** | No duplicate records in the analysis dataset | Composite key (facility_id + resident_id + event_date) must be unique | De-duplicate; log count of removed records |

### 3.3 KPI Calculation Pipeline (SQL Pattern)

Each KPI is computed via a standardized SQL view in BigQuery. Below is
the generalized template:

### 3.4 Example: 30-Day Hospital Readmission Rate (Monthly, Facility-Level)

> CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW oaltc_kpi.readmission_rate_monthly AS
>
> SELECT
>
> facility_id,
>
> facility_name,
>
> report_year,
>
> report_month,
>
> COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END) AS numerator,
>
> COUNT(\*) AS denominator,
>
> ROUND(SAFE_DIVIDE(COUNT(CASE WHEN readmitted_30d = TRUE THEN 1 END),
>
> COUNT(\*)) \* 100, 2) AS readmission_rate_pct,
>
> CASE
>
> WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) \* 100 \> 20 THEN ‘ALERT’
>
> WHEN SAFE_DIVIDE(…) \* 100 \> 15 THEN ‘WARNING’
>
> ELSE ‘ON TARGET’
>
> END AS performance_status
>
> FROM oaltc_raw.nh_discharge_events
>
> WHERE data_quality_flag = ‘PASS’
>
> AND discharge_date \>= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 13 MONTH)
>
> GROUP BY 1, 2, 3, 4;

## Section 4: Dashboard & Reporting Design

### 4.1 Dashboard Hierarchy

Three tiers of dashboards serve different audiences and decision-making
needs:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Tier** | **Dashboard Name** | **Primary Audience** | **KPIs Displayed** | **Refresh Cycle** |
| **Executive** | **OALTC Strategic Scorecard** | DOH Commissioner, OALTC Director | Tier 1 outcome & equity KPIs; trend lines; statewide maps | Monthly |
| **Program** | **Program Performance Monitor** | Bureau Chiefs, Program Managers | Tier 2 operational KPIs; facility rankings; alert flags; drill-downs | Weekly |
| **Operational** | **Data Operations Dashboard** | Analytics Team, IT, Data Stewards | Tier 3 data quality KPIs; pipeline status; submission compliance; error logs | Daily |

### 4.2 Standard Reporting Cadence

The following reporting schedule ensures stakeholders receive the right
information at the right time:

- Daily: Automated data quality alerts sent to Data Stewards for any
  pipeline failures, validation errors, or submission gaps. No manual
  action unless thresholds are breached.

- Weekly: Program Performance Monitor refreshed and shared with Bureau
  Chiefs. Includes a summary of KPIs in ALERT or WARNING status and any
  emerging trends.

- Monthly: Full KPI report package distributed to OALTC Program
  Directors. Includes trend analysis, month-over-month comparisons,
  facility-level rankings, and commentary on outliers.

- Quarterly: Strategic Scorecard presented to DOH senior leadership.
  Includes progress toward annual targets, equity gap analysis, and
  narrative summary for each strategic pillar.

- Annual: Year-end performance review document. Includes baseline
  resets, target revisions, lessons learned, and proposed additions or
  retirements to the KPI Registry.

### 4.3 Alert & Escalation Protocol

A tiered alert system ensures that performance signals translate into
timely action:

|  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|
| **Alert Level** | **Trigger Condition** | **Notification** | **Required Action** | **Timeline** |
| **⚠️ WARNING** | KPI exceeds 10% above target for one reporting period | Automated email to Program Manager and Data Steward | Analyst investigates root cause; documents findings in KPI log | Within 5 business days |
| **🔴 ALERT** | KPI exceeds warning threshold for two consecutive periods OR single-period breach is severe | Automated alert to Bureau Chief and Program Director; included in weekly summary | Bureau Chief reviews; corrective action plan initiated; escalated to OALTC Director if unresolved | Within 2 business days |
| **✅ ON TARGET** | KPI within or better than target range | Reflected in dashboard; highlighted in monthly report | No action required; document and share as best practice if sustained ≥ 3 months | Monthly review |

## Section 5: Advanced Analytics & Predictive Intelligence

### 5.1 Moving Beyond Descriptive KPIs

While standard KPI tracking captures what has happened, the Bureau of
Data Analytics and Automation can deliver significantly greater value by
layering predictive and explanatory analytics on top of the core KPI
framework. This transforms the system from a rearview mirror into an
early-warning and decision-support tool.

### 5.2 Predictive Modeling

- Ensemble machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost) can be
  trained on historical KPI trends to predict which facilities are at
  elevated risk of deteriorating performance in the next 30–90 days —
  enabling proactive intervention before a deficiency occurs.

- Time-series forecasting (ARIMA, Prophet, LSTM) can project KPI
  trajectories under different intervention scenarios, supporting
  resource allocation planning.

- Risk stratification models can flag facilities for prioritized
  oversight based on a composite risk score combining multiple KPIs,
  complaint history, and staffing data.

### 5.3 Explainable AI (XAI) for Root Cause Analysis

- SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values can identify which factors
  — staffing levels, ownership type, payer mix, geographic context — are
  the primary drivers of KPI variation across facilities.

- Geographically Weighted models can reveal whether the relationship
  between staffing and outcomes differs by region, enabling targeted
  policy responses rather than one-size-fits-all interventions.

### 5.4 Health Equity Analytics

- Stratified KPI analysis by race, ethnicity, payer type, and geography
  quantifies disparity gaps and tracks progress toward equity goals over
  time.

- Spatial clustering analysis (Moran’s I, LISA) can identify geographic
  hotspots of poor performance, directing inspection and support
  resources to underserved areas.

## Section 6: Stakeholder Engagement & Continuous Improvement

### 6.1 KPI Development Process

New KPIs are developed through a structured five-step process to ensure
relevance, feasibility, and buy-in:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **Step** | **Activity** | **Description** | **Responsible Party** |
| **1** | **Use Case Discovery** | Structured interviews and workshops with program offices to identify analytical needs and performance questions they cannot currently answer | Data Analyst 3 + Program Managers |
| **2** | **Data Feasibility Assessment** | Evaluate whether required data exists in BigQuery, the expected data quality, and any gaps that require new data feeds or collection instruments | Data Steward + IT |
| **3** | **KPI Definition & Review** | Draft formal KPI definition using the standard template; review with program office for accuracy and business relevance | Data Analyst 3 + Data Owner |
| **4** | **Pilot & Baseline** | Calculate the KPI for at least 12 months of historical data to establish baseline; review with stakeholders before setting targets | Data Analyst 3 |
| **5** | **Register & Deploy** | Add approved KPI to the KPI Registry, build the BigQuery view, connect to dashboard, and train program staff on interpretation | Data Steward + Data Analyst 3 |

### 6.2 Annual KPI Review Cycle

The KPI portfolio is reviewed annually to ensure ongoing relevance:

- Retire KPIs that are no longer aligned with strategic priorities or
  where the underlying program has changed.

- Revise targets based on actual performance trends, new benchmarks from
  CMS or peer states, and updated strategic goals.

- Add new KPIs identified through the use-case discovery process or
  driven by new data feeds coming online.

- Assess data quality trends for each KPI and invest in data improvement
  efforts for metrics showing persistent quality issues.

### 6.3 Capacity Building & Self-Service Analytics

A key goal is to build data literacy within OALTC program offices so
that staff can independently explore KPI data without relying solely on
the analytics team for every question:

- Develop user guides and short training modules for each dashboard,
  tailored to the non-technical program officer.

- Create a curated library of pre-built BigQuery queries that program
  staff can run directly for common ad-hoc questions.

- Host quarterly ‘Data Office Hours’ sessions where program staff can
  bring analytical questions and learn best practices for interpreting
  KPI trends.

## Section 7: Implementation Roadmap

The framework is implemented in four phases over 12 months:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
| **Phase** | **Timeline** | **Key Activities** | **Deliverables** |
| **Phase 1 Foundation** | Months 1–3 | Stakeholder interviews; data inventory; KPI Registry v1.0 (15–20 priority KPIs); BigQuery data quality audit; establish governance structure | KPI Registry; Governance Charter; Data Quality Baseline Report |
| **Phase 2 Core Build** | Months 4–6 | Build BigQuery transformation pipelines for Priority KPIs; deploy Operational Dashboard and Program Performance Monitor; set baselines and initial targets | Two live dashboards; 20 active KPI SQL views; Target-Setting Report |
| **Phase 3 Expansion** | Months 7–9 | Add equity KPI layer; build Executive Scorecard; deploy predictive risk model for facility oversight prioritization; launch staff training program | Executive Scorecard; Equity KPI Module; Risk Stratification Model |
| **Phase 4 Maturity** | Months 10–12 | Annual KPI review; refine alert thresholds based on operational experience; expand self-service analytics; document full framework for handover and sustainability | Updated KPI Registry; Year-1 Performance Report; Sustainability Plan |

This framework provides OALTC with a scalable, evidence-based foundation
for performance management. By combining rigorous KPI governance, a
robust BigQuery data architecture, tiered dashboards, and predictive
analytics, the Bureau of Data Analytics and Automation can move from
reactive reporting to proactive program stewardship — ultimately
improving outcomes for New York’s aging and long-term care population.
